content.title: Arizona coach Tommy Lloyd doesn’t need the next job
content.text: SAN JOSE, Calif. — Tommy Lloyd waited 20 years to be this popular. That’s how we view it, at least. The blind ambition and transactional nature of men’s college basketball encourage such a mindset. It’s a disease, really. But Lloyd seems different.Is it possible to be different?The Arizona coach has developed the most complete team in this NCAA Tournament. With a 109-88 victory over Arkansas on Thursday night, the Wildcats (35-2) advanced to the Elite Eight for the first time in Lloyd’s five seasons in Tucson. It happened amid speculation that he is a coveted candidate for the North Carolina job, one of the sport’s rarest jewels.The mere perception of interest — and the terrible timing — puts Lloyd in a no-win situation. Yet winning is his only concern.He never craved this kind of attention. He wanted to build a coaching career, team by team, task by task. For two decades, he worked as an assistant for Mark Few at Gonzaga, doing his job rather than auditioning for a bigger one. He carved out a niche in international recruiting. He became a complete coach. He never let career aspiration overtake sound judgment.Five years ago, he was offered the right job, a chance to lead a fabled Wildcats program recovering from a federal bribery scandal. Now, Arizona is Arizona again. Lloyd didn’t rebuild. He took over. The man has a 147-35 record, three Sweet 16s and one Elite Eight that may upgrade to a Final Four come Saturday night if the Wildcats can defeat Purdue.Of course, North Carolina should want him.Is it possible he’s too focused to care?“There’s not one thing that is going to knock me off my path,” Lloyd said when asked about North Carolina before the Arkansas game.Then his team went out and shot 63.8 percent and scored triple digits despite attempting just eight 3-pointers.“I already have one of the best jobs in the country,” said Lloyd, who is trying to lead Arizona to its first Final Four in 25 years. “And one thing we talk about in our program all the time — and I think I’ve gotten better at it, and I think our team’s been crushing it this year — is just the ability to have full focus and be present in the moment.”In this game, Arizona mastered mindfulness. The Wildcats stayed present even when Arkansas got chippy and turned the final eight minutes into a series of confrontations. Coach John Calipari was whistled for a technical foul. Billy Richmond III was ejected after committing a flagrant 2 foul. Unable to prevent Arizona from getting to the rim, the Razorbacks committed several hard fouls in frustration.The Wildcats barely flinched. They showed a little irritation and commenced domination.“We want to play championship basketball,” said Lloyd, whose staff warned the players that the game could get nasty. “To play championship basketball, you’ve got to just stand up and walk away from the action. This isn’t the playground, you know what I mean? You can’t just throw down. That’s not how you win basketball games. These guys have high character and they’re winners, but they’re competitors, and it’s always a fine line for both teams.”Lloyd knows this is a special team. The Wildcats are the best squad remaining. The margin isn’t large, but there is a gap when you add together Arizona’s size in the frontcourt, playmaking in the backcourt and the versatility throughout its eight-man rotation. It can win a track meet or a wrestling match.In some ways, this team is reminiscent of the balanced Florida roster that spurred the Gators to a national title last season. But the top of Arizona’s roster is even more formidable. That doesn’t guarantee the Wildcats a championship. Still, it’s an opportunity that comes along once a decade. Lloyd has been near the top of the sport for all five of his seasons, as evidenced by his NCAA Tournament seeds: 1, 2, 2, 4 and 1. Despite the consistency, he has never been this close to the ultimate prize. Everyone feels the vibe.“This is the most fun I’ve had playing basketball, honestly,” freshman forward Koa Peat said.Six Arizona players scored at least 14 points against Arkansas. No team in NCAA Tournament history had done that. No one took more than 11 shots. The Wildcats are an efficiency machine.“Of all the matchups that I didn’t want to see, it was this one,” Calipari said.Arizona was too big for Arkansas. And Lloyd is too locked in.Your browser does not support the video tag.0:00 / 0:41At this time of year, perspective can get distorted. Coaches start thinking several steps ahead, even when they insist they aren’t, even when they have so much to play for. That’s how the sport is wired. There is always another negotiation, another job, another climb. But greatness cannot be achieved with divided attention.Arizona isn’t overpowering in a single area. It is overwhelming because there’s no obvious place to attack. Too big. Too creative. Enough shooting. Enough toughness. Elite chemistry. That kind of balance is built over time, with intention and with vision.It reflects the efforts of a clear-minded coach. Lloyd didn’t skip steps to get here. He didn’t chase visibility or leverage every triumph. He’s in the moment, learning, getting better. That doesn’t make him immune to wanting more, whether that’s North Carolina or another gig down the line. It just means he understands what he has right now.“You don’t have hubris,” he said of his approach. “You understand how hard this is.”Going back to his time at Gonzaga, Lloyd has been a part of consistent excellence. Still, this is something else. This is what it looks like when nothing — and no one — is pulling in a different direction.Now, Lloyd must answer to that standard. His standard. This is the moment he wanted for so long. Maximize it, and there’s no reason to want anything besides longevity.“Listen, I read this in a book,” Lloyd said. “What was the best candy bar in 1946?”The answer was Snickers.“What’s the best, the most popular candy bar today?” he said. “Same as ever. I haven’t flinched. I’m playing the same exact style we learned at Gonzaga that I brought to Arizona. I’m doubling down on it. I’m not worried about trends. I never look at trends. I’m like, ‘What do I think is the most effective way for my team to play, and what are my strengths as a coach?’“You gotta play into that. Why would I try to reinvent myself as a coach when this has been pretty effective? Can I get better at it? Can we double down on our strengths?”He’s disciplined enough to stay in the present. This team, his masterpiece, exemplifies that quality.For now, Lloyd can see only what’s in front of him. He won’t look beyond. The moment is enough.
